utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-00-39-T, The Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Before we invite the Prosecution to call its next witness, I would like to deliver two oral decisions. The first one is a decision on the Prosecution's motion for protective measures at trial for Witness 666, a witness known under another pseudonym, another pseudonym in another case. In accordance with Article 21 of the Statute and Rule 75(A) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Chamber may order measures for protection of witnesses provided that the measures are consistent with the rights of the accused. To order protective measures, the Chamber must be satisfied on the basis of information provided by the Prosecution that the circumstances justify withholding information from the public. In its decision of the 11th of December 2003, the Chamber ordered that Witness 66 be referred to by pseudonym and ordered the delayed disclosure of the transcripts of the witness's interviews and of related exhibits. The Prosecution now requests image and voice distortion for the witness's testimony and that he be permitted to testify in private session for those portions of his testimony that are reasonably likely to reveal his identity. In the Defence response filed on the 19th of July this year and in the further response filed on the 26th of July, the Defence opposed the motions on the grounds that the information thus far disclosed to the Defence did not satisfy the Prosecution's burden of proof for the imposition of the additional protective measures. The Chamber has considered the information submitted by the Prosecution on Witness 666. The Chamber is satisfied that the witness's family has received serious threats to their security and that the witness has a genuine fear of reprisals against his relatives and against himself should it become known that he testified before the Tribunal. The Chamber is further satisfied that the protective measures requested strike an appropriate balance between the rights of the accused to a public trial and the protection of Witness 666 and his family. The protective measures in question are hereby granted and the Trial Chamber requests Madam Registrar to convey to the Victims and Witnesses Unit the content of this decision. The second decision to be delivered is a decision on the Defence application for certification. It's an application by the Defence for certification to appeal the Chamber's oral decision of the 30th of July dismissing the Defence Motion of the 23rd of July on translation of transcripts and other documents into B/C/S. Rule 73(B) of the Rules states that a Trial Chamber may grant certification for interlocutory appeal if the impugned decision involves an issue that would significantly affect the fair and expeditious conduct of the proceedings or the outcome of the trial and for which in the opinion of the Trial Chamber an immediate resolution by the Appeals Chamber may materially advance the proceedings. In its application, the Defence asserts that two criteria of Rule 73(B) are met. The Defence claims that in the first place the issue of translation goes to the heart of Mr. Krajisnik's ability to defend himself adequately through his counsel. Accordingly, the Defence continues, it impacts directly on the fairness of the trial and is clearly capable of significantly affecting the outcome of the trial. As to the second criteria, the Defence claims that Mr. Krajisnik's ability to work with certain types of printed documents including transcripts of the current proceedings in his own language will improve the efficient presentation of his Defence. The Defence asserts that this will benefit all participants in this trial in the search for the truth and will therefore in itself materially advance the proceedings. On the 17th of August, the Prosecution filed a response asking the Chamber to deny the application. In the Chamber's opinion, the Defence has failed to make a case on the first criterion. It has failed to show that Mr. Krajisnik's access to B/C/S audiorecordings of the proceedings, that his lack of access to hard copy transcriptions of those recordings constitutes a deficiency which would significantly affect the fair and expeditious conduct of the proceeding or the outcome of the trial. Chamber recognised in its decision that Mr. Krajisnik would perhaps be able to more efficiently had he had access to transcriptions of the B/C/S recordings, but lesser efficiency is not necessarily a handicap which rises to the level of significantly affecting the fairness of the proceedings. The Defence has not shown that this presumed lesser efficiency has that effect in the present case. In the impugned decision, the Chamber reiterated the operative principle that the guarantees provided in Article 21, Section 4 of the Statute do not extend to all documents, but only to evidence which forms the basis of the determination by the Chamber of the charges against the accused and that this right is ensured inter alia by the fact that all evidence admitted at trial is provided in a language the accused understands. This principle is fully complied with in the present proceedings. What the Defence is asking for is more than this. It's asking for the translated material to be supplied in a certain format and it is asking for the essentially routine translation of a variety of material on top of the material proposed for admission as evidence. The case law of the Tribunal, including the Celebici, Naletelic and Kvocka cases, the first case, the decision of the 25th of September, 1996 in Naletelic, the decision of the 18th of October 2001, and in Kvocka, the decision on Goran Zigic Motion for translation of documents pertaining to his appeal of the 3rd of October 2001, the cases cited in the Chamber's impugned decision supports the conclusion that the Chamber is complying with this principle. To meet the burden of the first criterion of Rule 73(B) the Defence would need to show that the Chamber decision, though complying with the case law of the Tribunal, breaches an established principle of fairness as expressed in Article 21 of the Statute, but no such principle has been put forth by the Defence, nor has the Defence shown that the Chamber's decision may have breached the principle I read out a moment ago. Since the Defence has not made out the first criterion of the certification rule, the Chamber does not need to consider the Defence submission on the second criterion. The Defence application therefore is dismissed. These are the two decisions I'd like to deliver to you. Another issue that has been very much on the mind of the Chamber, both before the recess and also after the recess, was the pace in which we were operating in this case, apart from times not used to sit, days not used to sit, because on the average only 1.8 hours a day were used for examination-in-chief. This is not to blame one of the parties, but rather it's just something important to establish. The Chamber refrains, however, from further considering this matter at this very moment, although it will certainly further monitor this matter. Since it's the experience of the Chamber that not only during the last two days, but also during the last two days, that the parties better and better managed to examine the witness within the estimated time, even more and more often now considerably within the estimate given, and the Defence is keeping well within the limits of the -- what I would call the 60 per cent rule for the cross-examination. Therefore the Chamber at this moment feels that it's wiser to encourage the parties to continue. If I look at the last two days, the time scheduled for examination-in-chief was seven hours. That would add another four hours for cross-examination. That would take 11 hours. But the two witnesses were -- the examination of the two witnesses was concluded not only within the eight hours we were sitting these two days, but even within the even lesser number of hours available since we also had to deal with a few procedural issues. So the Chamber decided that it would encourage the parties to continue in this way to use the time in court as efficiently as possible. These were the procedural issues the Chamber would like to raise at this moment. There might come a few more during the coming days. Therefore, I'd like to invite the Prosecution, and if I do understand well, it will be Ms. Karagiannakis who will examine the next witness. Is that correct? Ms. Karagiannakis, now you are also introduced already on the record for reasons of the transcript. Madam Usher, could you please -- yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, good morning, and it's very nice to be back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, good afternoon. It's very nice to be back even in the afternoon, Your Honour, and thank you. I -- what Your Honour just said over the last few moments sounded suspiciously like a compliment to those that were dealing with the matter in court the last couple of days so I am certainly delighted on the Defence's behalf to hear the Trial Chamber's approval of the way in which the matter has been dealt with. The -- just a couple of matters. I had proposed to be here, which is just mentioned as a courtesy to Your Honour, just for the first session today, but I am dealing then with the next two witnesses. So I promise I'll be back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- I did mention to Mr. Harmon this morning, not -- I didn't see him or speak to him, but I just sent him an email that in relation to one matter, which is a Prosecution motion in relation to a witness with the number 623 in this case. That's for protective measures. There's a motion on the table for protective measures, that there is a reference in that motion to a decision of the Tribunal which was made on the 5th of April -- was it this year? 5th of April this year. It was made on an ex parte application. I understand it was a confidential decision. We have not been supplied with it. My understanding is that I should ask the Trial Chamber for that decision to be made available to us, which I therefore do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Unless Mr. Harmon would think that whether reasons why he asked for an ex-parte decision at that time do not exist any more. Sometimes, for example, delayed disclosure is something you would apply for ex parte, but if it comes to protective measures and if the date comes close to where the witness will testify, the delay has found his end, and then of course there might be under circumstances, it might not be necessary for the Chamber to interfere, but that the Prosecution could at that time then disclose the existence of such a decision to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That helps me, Your Honour. I had not understood, but it may be that my misunderstanding is therefore being corrected. I had not understood that it was within the Prosecution's unilateral power simply to release to us a decision which was given as a confidential decision. If it is, then we shall in future then simply apply in the first place to the Prosecution and only trouble the Trial Chamber if there is an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, it depends on the reasons why a decision was given ex parte. But delayed disclosure is one of the -- I would say one of the typical decisions where at a certain moment, the -- it's not needed any more to keep something secret because then disclosure will take place anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm slightly -- I was puzzled. I had a discussion with one of our legal assistants this morning. It seemed to me, unless I've got it wrong, to be two completely different concepts. One is ex parte where the application is made ex parte without reference to the other party, and the other is when the decision is actually given as a confidential decision, the two being strictly speaking different things. If it has -- is given as a confidential decision, and my understanding was that it -- maybe I'm wrong about that, but it's then not within the unilateral power of the Prosecution to waive that or release it. But we would at the very least have to make, it might be a fairly formal step on occasions, but at the very least have to have the approval of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If a decision is given only confidentially, then it's usually known to the parties. And if it's ex parte and confidential, then it would be different. But confidentiality does not exclude one of parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I'm not making myself clear. When the application is made ex parte, as it was, then by definition we were not there and were not involved. If the decision on that ex parte application is then a confidential decision, we have not received it because it was an ex parte application. But we -- again, unless I've misunderstood it, the fact that the decision was then given as a confidential decision means that it's only the Trial Chamber that can then release the decision from that confidentiality and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From the ex parte character or --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, the ex parte character is a sense what -- if it started off as confidential, if it was a confidential decision, confidential to those that were party to that application, then that's only the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore -- if then a decision would be given ex parte and confidential, that would be double. There would be no need. It's my understanding of the system of this Tribunal, but I'm also looking at the Registrar, that if a decision is given ex parte that means that the other party is not involved or even aware, perhaps, of the application that was at the basis of the decision. It's sometimes from the very nature of the reasons why the application was made ex parte, it becomes clear that if certain conditions are fulfilled, that the Prosecution in my view could lift that ex parte character. And, of course, the question is whether they would need leave by the Trial Chamber to do that. I think it never causes any damage if you ask, but whether they would need it even under the circumstances as I just described, that's not -- that doesn't go without saying as far as I'm concerned. But even if then the Prosecution would say, well, let's say, the late disclosure of a protected witness, the disclosure has to take place within 30 days before the witness has testified and the witness is supposed to be called at the 1st of October, then on from the 1st of September, there would be no need to keep that decision ex parte any more because the other party would ask themselves why they didn't receive that material any earlier. So it even makes sense. But then still the decision would still be confidential to the extent that the outside world would not know about its contents, would not know about who is granted what pseudonym, et cetera. So ex parte and confidential can exist next to each other. But let's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say, I'll read the transcript tonight to see whether I can understand what on earth any of this is about. It's taking me a while to get into the swing of it. The -- but the key point actually, and the -- whatever the precise procedure, Your Honour, is, may we with whoever's permission is required, may we see this decision of the 5th of April 2000 which at the moment is not available and has not been available to us without which we can't fully understand the motion to which we now have to respond. And whoever is empowered to give that permission on that release, may we have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I haven't got, of course, the decision clearly in my mind. Mr. Tieger, could you -- it's printed out for me at this very moment but if you answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The answer is relatively simply, Your Honour. And that is that the premise that underlines -- underlies the request, I think, is faulty. The motion before the Court at this point, the motion that was filed on August 24th, is not predicated in any manner on the previous ruling. It stands on its own and can be understood on its own, responded to on its own, and ruled on on its own. And no previous filing, confidential, ex parte or not, is needed in order to formulate a response.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That takes us slightly by surprise since the decision is expressly referred to and footnoted in the motion. But if the position is that nobody will look at that decision, neither the Trial Chamber nor the Prosecution nor anybody else, and it will be completely disregarded and all its contents completely disregarded for the purpose of deciding the motion, then I'm entirely content. But if that's not the position, then I'll press my application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'll check that. Of course, if it's of no importance for understanding the motion, if it's fully apart, then of course one would wonder why to mention it in the application at all. But we'll have a look at it. It's printed out to me now. It's confidential and ex parte. Any further issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I wasn't here on Monday when I noticed -- though in private session, I noticed that my name was taken either in vain or was certainly mentioned on occasions. There was an issue. I -- I'm -- we're in open session at the moment. I certainly don't propose to trespass into any sensitive areas, though I must say I didn't see very many in that private session on the transcript as it happens. But I just wanted to assure Your Honours that I am going to take the earliest reasonable opportunity to speak to Mr. Krajisnik again about such matters. I'm going to see him tomorrow afternoon, and I will do my very best to resolve such factual and other issues as arise in relation to that matter. I just wanted to make one thing clear, though, with respect, so there is no misunderstanding, because one of the points -- and I don't believe this is a sensitive matter which is inappropriate for me to mention in open session, Your Honour, was the question of proceeding now and I think Your Honour mentioned an issue which the Trial Chamber didn't wish to get into which was the professional responsibilities and professional ethics. As far as we are concerned, the Defence counsel, the position is very clear. We have the conduct of the case. And as long as we are counsel on the case, we will proceed in the normal way according to the normal criteria so that unless there is some reason according to the normal criteria why we would apply to the Tribunal for further time before we proceed with cross-examination or unless there's some reason why we should decide not to cross-examine, which of course is a perfectly normal decision that one might take, that we will proceed according to the normal criteria. And so Your Honour can assume safely that there will be cross-examination of all the witnesses who are programmed to come up over the next few days. Whether it's short or long, that's another matter but we will proceed with, of course, as I have mentioned, the usual way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for this information.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just before the next witness is brought into the courtroom, there is one matter I should place on the record. At 10.30 last night, the Prosecution forwarded their summary in relation to the last witness via email. And then also in addition a supplementary information sheet. Now, I think that whilst I don't have a problem with material being forwarded at a late stage by the Prosecution or -- the Defence are under enormous pressure. At the same time, a summary at 10.30 at night, which of course I received this morning because I tend not to be on the internet late into the evening, is inappropriate. And I would like to think that if it could be avoided in the future it should be avoided in the future. I think a marker was put down by the Defence at some point that perhaps if a summary could be delivered perhaps by 9.00 the previous evening. The other aspect is this, and I don't blame Ms. Karagiannakis for this, I mean we're all under a lot of pressure, but it would be preferable if we could get this material earlier to ensure that we are efficient in court. Secondly, the supplementary information sheet is not a short one. There are two pages of material. That's in addition to the summary. And I would indicate this: That, Your Honour, I cannot guarantee that I will commence my cross-examination once the evidence in chief of this witness has been completed today. I will make that decision as the evidence progresses and as the additional material is interpolated into the evidence in chief. And, of course, we do have other matters that we can go on with. But Your Honour would be aware that the Defence does not have the luxury that the Prosecution has. For example, this week of having a different Prosecution counsel for every witness. And I place that on the record, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. Now, whether that's only a luxury or whether there are other reasons behind that is another matter. But may I take it, and I'm addressing you, Mr. Tieger, because, of course, I could ask you for explanations, et cetera. May I take it that this happened in the first week after the recess and that we are not facing all kind of practical consequences due to the fact that the summaries have not been provided in due time, and I think 9.00 the prior evening is a -- is already a very generous situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, you can certainly assume that -- well, first of all, I don't know the extent to which the recess and the resumption played a role. But I wouldn't be at all surprised if it did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It gave you a way out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I -- and of course, the Court is aware, we will make every effort to ensure that the summaries are provided as early in the process as possible. Furthermore, when it -- that proves not to be the case for some reason, we will try to work as closely with the Defence to ensure that it doesn't handicap the process any more than absolutely necessary and we will certainly try to wrest the underlying reasons that might cause such a delay if it were to occur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. That is a long sentence for it will not happen again. Ms. Karagiannakis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Can I just add a few words by explanation, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but few words.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Just a few words. Well, in relation to the additional information, obviously, I only saw the witness beginning yesterday morning. So I wasn't in a position to conclude and provide that additional information until after I'd seen the witness. In relation to the summary, yes, we will endeavour to have those summaries done beforehand. But of course, the summary is not the evidence in the case. It's simply something we're reading out for the purpose of the public record. And the evidence in this case, we'll seek to have two statements of the witness admitted pursuant to the 89 -- Rule 89(F) procedure, and of course they have been in the possession of the Defence for some time now, I think, from at least the 17th of August. I just wanted to add those few brief comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Let's not -- I do understand that you can't get any additional information until you've seen the witness. On the other hand, then you have to take care that you see the witness at such a time that the additional information reaches the Defence in time. Because I do agree that under Rule 89(F) it might be less traumatic, but if new information comes in, it should be there in time in order to enable the Defence to make any further inquiries as necessary. So the mere fact that you couldn't give it before you had spoken to the witness is not very convincing. Let's proceed. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. Ms. Karagiannakis, I do understand there are no protective measures in effect and that your next witness is Mr. Osmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Osmanovic, at least I take it you are Mr. Osmanovic, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of this solemn declaration is handed out to you now by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Osmanovic. Please be seated. You'll first be examined by Ms. Karagiannakis, counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed, Ms. Karagiannakis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: As I said, Your Honour, we will be seeking to introduce two statements through the Rule 89(F) procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, would you please give them a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The witness statement dated 5, 7, and 10 October 1994 will be Prosecution Number P265. The statement dated the 7th of June 2001 will be Prosecution Exhibit Number P266.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. What's the original, in this case, Ms. Karagiannakis? Is that the English, as usual? So then the B/C/S translation would get P265.1 and P266.1. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Karagiannakis:

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Could the witness be provided with the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With his statements, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, can you see the two ICTY statements in front of you?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise these statements as statements you've given to the representatives of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to review these statements yesterday before today's court proceedings?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you satisfied that these statements are a correct and accurate -- are correct and accurate, and are you willing to confirm to this Court that's the case?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I did give these statements, and they are correct and accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: At this stage, I would like to move for the admission of P265 and 266.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We usually decide at the very end on the admission into evidence. And the supplemental information sheet is not at this moment --

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: I chose not to introduce it through the 89(F) procedure because of the delivery last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: I propose to read out a summary of these statements. And then I will ask some additional questions clarifying what's in the statements, and then leading the additional information that the witness provided yesterday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic was living and working in the Municipality of Vlasenica in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1990. From August 1991 to April 1992, he noticed an increase in Serb nationalism and noticed that Serbs and Muslims were starting to divide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Karagiannakis, you know that when you're reading, usually the speed of speech goes up. Would you please slow down a bit for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Little bit rusty. On or about the 23rd or 24th of April 1992, the JNA took over most of the vital departments in the town, including defence, justice, bank, post office, and police. The witness believes that prior to the -- sorry, the witness states that prior to the conflict, the SDS and the JNA were working together. After the takeover, a local Serb called Milakovic who was a member of the SDS assisted the JNA by assisting in the mobilisations of the local Serbs into the JNA. Local Serbs assisted the JNA by collecting weapons and manning checkpoints. Milomir Stanic was appointed mayor of Vlasenica before the war and became head of the SDS Crisis Staff. The witness says in his statement that the SDS Crisis Staff governed the municipality after the takeover and the departure of the JNA. Stanic was in charge of all civil and military departments in Vlasenica. Directly under him were Milenko Djuric, in charge of civil departments, and Kraljevic, who was in charge of military departments, including Serb special forces. Basic reported to Kraljevic. The witness saw Basic at Susica giving lists of names to Dragan Nikolic of prisoners to be transported to Batkovic camp in Bijeljina Municipality. The witness also saw Kraljevic at Susica. Dragan Nikolic reported to Kraljevic and Basic. The Susica camp guards reported to the camp commander Dragan Nikolic. The local president of the SDS was Milomir Lukic. The headquarters for the special forces and the crisis committee was the bauxite premises. After the takeover in April and May 1992, Muslims were not allowed to withdraw all their money from the bank. They were only allowed to withdraw a restricted amount, whereas people of Serb ethnicity had unrestricted access to their money. Muslims working at the bauxite company did not receive their monthly salary in May 1992 whereas Serb coworkers did. Muslims were scared to open their stores after the takeover as they found that the stores of Muslims who had left Vlasenica had been broken into and had signs painted on their shops and houses reading, "Muslims leave", I quote, and, I quote, "We will kill all Ustasha". Between 22nd April and 22nd May 1992, the non-Serb population was not allowed to move freely within the municipality or to leave it. Transit permits to move within the town were issued at the municipality building. The permits were headed Serb Municipality of Vlasenica-Crisis Staff, and signed -- and were signed by Stanic. The Crisis Staff also announced that the residents would lose their jobs in Vlasenica if they did not return to work. The witness saw another Crisis Staff order signed by Stanic as president of the Crisis Staff to the 10 August company telling the company to provide wooden boards to the army. When the regular forces of the JNA left Vlasenica on or about 17 or 18 of May, they left all their equipment behind to the local Serbs who used this equipment to shell a number of nearby villages. The shells were incendiary and were designed to burn houses. As a result of the shelling, some Muslims were killed, and the remainder of the Muslim population fled. After his arrest on the 22nd of May, the witness was taken to the police station with 20 other Muslim detainees. He was subjected to beatings with police batons, metal pipes, and metal chains by special military police. He saw other detainees being repeatedly beaten with metal pipes chains, and grip portions of guns over the following days. Whilst at the police station he witnessed the murder of Mr. Ambeskovic who was a Muslim who had organised the referendum for a separate Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mr. Osmanovic was held there for 11 days before being transferred on the 2nd of June to Vlasenica prison. It had the capacity to hold 50 men, but actually held about 150 Muslim men. Upon arrival, his valuables were taken away. He was regularly beaten at Vlasenica prison, and many detainees were taken out and never returned. While at the prison, he was taken to help bury 22 villagers killed in the Muslim village of Drum on the outskirts of Vlasenica. All were male, and all but one had a single bullet hole in the middle of the forehead. The witness was then taken to Susica camp on the 18th of June 1992 which then held about 500 to 550 people of which six or seven were women.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please make a break. Please pause for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: The oldest woman was about 80 years old. Susica camp was run by Dragan Nikolic. He told detainees he was God and law, and the guards reported to him. The witness saw two of the detainees taken out of the hangar by Nikolic. They were beaten so badly that shortly after their return they died from their injuries. He also saw a detainee called Reuf beaten so badly over a four or five day period that he begged to be killed. Nikolic, however, told him that a bullet cost 3 deutschemarks. Nikolic mistreated prisoners by threatening them with a tear gas canister, firing his weapon, placing a pistol in the mouth of a detainee and continually beating them. The witness was forced by guards to leave the camp and loot Muslim property. Mr. Osmanovic was transferred to Batkovic prison on the 30th of June 1992 where he was remained for 13 months. Upon arrival at Batkovic camp, Mr. Osmanovic was beaten by the guards and remaining valuables were taken. He witnessed several beatings including one of a 70-year-old man who died as a result of the beatings he received. In addition to the guards, policemen from Zenica participated in the beatings. Several detainees, in particular older people, died as a result of their mistreatment in Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You changed two times at least the word "believes." And"that he states". I tried to check. Is that -- of course, that's a different content of a summary. Is -- the one read out is the more correct one? Or is --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I can indicate, Your Honour, that I actually objected to the use of the term "belief" within the summary. As I understood it, Ms. Karagiannakis was going to insert rather than "he believes," "in his statement, the witness states that he believes." That was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, we can check in the statement whether in the statement whether believe is expressed or whether in the statement any observation of facts is...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, the statement does contain "beliefs," you see. And that's why -- of course I'm uncomfortable with the use of the term "belief" but if we're going to use the term "belief" in a summary in the evidence, I think it should be made abundantly clear that what the statement contains is -- that the witness statements contains a statement of belief. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Karagiannakis, was it your intention to summarise by saying "the witness stated that" or that "stated as his belief that"?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: It's just a summary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please put your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Pardon me, Your Honour. It's just a summary of the witness statement. I believe that we will be addressing this during -- throughout the course of this, so I'm going to take the witness directly to the relevant sections and ask him what it is he is saying and why it is that he is saying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The statements are tendered into evidence and the only reason why I'm asking for it is in order to have a clear picture for the public who has, of course, to rely on the summary read by you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, could you please look at paragraph 7 and 8 of your statement dated 7 June 2001. Do you see those paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those paragraphs deal with the issue of transit passes. Can you please read those two paragraphs and just clarify for us what type of passes were available to people in Vlasenica between the 22nd of April and the 22nd of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: All the Muslims in Vlasenica, between the 22nd April and 22 May when I was taken to prison, those who wanted to leave the municipality of Vlasenica and go to Kladanj and Zivinice got a transit pass from the Crisis Staff. Those who remained in town got a pass which allowed them to move about to their fields, to their work. There were two types of passes. One was the so-called local pass, and the other one was the so-called transit pass.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, why were -- you say here in your statement, this is the non-Serb population applying for these passes. That's paragraph 7. Why were they asking for these passes?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Primarily for their own security. While these passes were being issued, the transit passes, that is certificates allowing people to go and leave Vlasenica and those allowing people to move about Vlasenica, the able-bodied men were taken too the police station where they were interrogated and beaten. Then they would return. Some managed to leave Vlasenica during that time. Some remained in Vlasenica. Those who trusted the SDS, the Crisis Staff and the local Serbs, remained in Vlasenica. Unfortunately, many of them never managed to leave it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of people got passes to leave the municipality?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Transit passes were given only to women, children, children who were minors, and elderly, over the 65 years of age. The able-bodied men could not get those passes unless they had some very good strings to pull or unless they had money to pay for those passes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, you said that you got a transit pass, and you've just told us that there were two types of transit passes. What type of transit pass did you get?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I got a transit pass which allowed me to move about Vlasenica and to go to my field which was some 3 kilometres away. On the way there, I had to pass the checkpoint which was manned by the local Serbs. So in other words, this transit pass allowed me to go to my house, to my field, and to my work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe the contents of that pass to the Court.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: It said "pass, the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Vlasenica," and pass for the person whose name was mentioned, and movement is allowed within the boundaries of the municipality or it is allowed to the bearer of the pass to leave the municipality. At the bottom of the pass, there was a stamp of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Vlasenica, and the signature was of Mr. Stanic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have that pass with you here today?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown the next exhibit, which is marked with number 03010815.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit Number P267.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, can you please look at the B/C/S version of this pass that's before you and please tell the Court in what ways is it similar to the pass that was issued to you and in what ways if any is it different from the pass that was issued to you?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a pass identical to mine. There's just one difference. And that is the handwritten words "this is a pass allowing the bearer to leave Vlasenica and travel to Zivinice." In my case, it said the movement is allowed on route Vlasenica-Bregovi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose signature was on the pass that was issued to you?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Milenko Stanic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I've concluded with that exhibit. Mr. Osmanovic, the next set of questions I'm going to ask you relate to your statement dated 5, 7, and 10 October 1994. Can you please put that before and look at paragraph 65. In that paragraph, and I'm summarising, you say that the Crisis Staff made all the final decisions in the town. Then you say that the president of the Crisis Staff was in charge because you saw his name on orders. Then you tell us about two orders. The last part of that paragraph reads -- tells us about an order that "the Crisis Staff committee also publicised that residents would lose their jobs in Vlasenica if they did not return to work." Then you say "I saw his name on this order and I had to note all the Muslims who did not return to work in my section." Can you please tell us in more detail what precisely was said in this announcement.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: It appeared in the 10th August company where I was employed. A paper was put in which it said that the Crisis Staff of Vlasenica Municipality orders Muslims to return to work, those who were absent from work for three days would lose their jobs. And it also said that a certain amount of timber had to be surrendered to the army and the signature on that notice was that of Stanic. And one more addition, something that I heard was that a megaphone was used on a police vehicle to inform the Muslim population to go back to work. Otherwise, they would lose their work and their property. The SDS, the Crisis Staff guaranteed full security to all the population of non-Serbian origin. This announcement was read from a police vehicle via a megaphone, and the previous two announcements were in a written form.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've got a number of questions. First of all, in relation to the written announcements, did you see any stamps on those announcements?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: It was the Crisis Staff stamp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see any signature on those announcements?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The signature, again, Stanic's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were those announcements posted? When did you see them?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I saw them when I arrived at work in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which morning was that?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Before that, we started working from 6.00. And after the curfew was introduced, we started working at 8.00. A lot of people lived far away from Vlasenica, and if they wanted to be on time for work, they had to start during the dark because of the curfew, the working hours were moved forward. I arrived around half past 7.00. Two or three days after --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, go ahead. Sorry, go ahead. You're getting to the point now.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: It was two, three days after the factory started working because the factory was closed for two or three days after the JNA and the local Serbs took over the power in the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in relation to the announcement that you heard, did you personally hear it or did somebody tell you that they heard it?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard it myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard it on my way back home from work. People were invited to come back. I don't know how people in Zivinice heard about that. They managed to return to Vlasenica. They heard that the SDS and the Crisis Staff guaranteed full security. Some people from Zivinice returned to Vlasenica. They managed to get to the municipal prison, and from there they never returned alive. They never got out of there alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you trust the message that was put out in that announcement?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I did unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your safety guaranteed?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I believed so. That was my impression. However, my impression was wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please now look at the first -- look at the same paragraph, and you make a statement there. You say, paragraph 65, the crisis committee appeared to make all the final decisions in the town. Then you quote those examples. Are there any other reasons why you draw that conclusion apart from the reasons that you've stated in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that there is. When the Serbian autonomous province of Bihac was established, before Bosnia and Herzegovina was proclaimed an independent state, a plebiscite was organised for the Serbian People who voted in favour of staying in Yugoslavia. SAO Krajina, SAO Romanija, and SAO Bihac were formed before that. And Vlasenica, Srebrenica, Bratunac, Sekovici municipality together with Zvornik were included in the Bihac Serbian autonomous province. There was a dual authority. There was a legal municipality of Vlasenica, and in the Milici, the former local commune, there was a so-called Serbian Municipality of Vlasenica with its seat in Milici. So there was a dual power. When the JNA and the local Serbs entered Vlasenica, the Crisis Staff arrived in Vlasenica in the headquarters of the bauxite mine, and whatever was done from then on was done through the Crisis Staff, nobody else. The Crisis Staff was the leading body, the body which had power in the -- during the imminent threat of war as they said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you please tell the Court how you come to know the facts about the political situation that you've just described.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: This was broadcast on television, and this could also be read in the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you please look at paragraph 64 of that statement. There you say that you believe Stanic was in charge of all civil and military departments in Vlasenica, and then you go on to describe a command structure, so to speak. Could you please tell the Court: What is the basis of your opinion in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia, the army had its own system, and they controlled the Territorial Defence Staff, and they didn't interfere with the civilian affairs. The former police had its own system, and they didn't interfere with the army dealings. All the people wearing uniform reported to the commander of the police station. The inspectors and people working in civilian clothes reported to the chief of the police station, the chief of police station was in charge of those. In the military hierarchy, it is well-known that a lower-ranking officer reports to higher-ranking officers. In the Susica camp, when there was the first transport of people from -- to Batkovic, I saw Veljko Basic giving a list to Basic [as interpreted], and he told him, Kraljevic is my commander. When Kraljevic arrived, Kraljevic greeted Basic in the military way although Basic was a former policeman. After that, Nikolic also used the military greetings, the military salute, and that's where I draw my conclusion from about the hierarchy that existed. Vojo Nikolic who I mentioned here used to be a teacher, and then he started working in the police station as an instructor. He worked with the uniformed police, and among these people who are mentioned here, he was the only one who had some education, and he was a regular police officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just stop you there. It may well be something incorrect in the translation, but it says here that "at Batkovic I saw Basic giving a list to Basic", and then he told him "Krajisnik is my commander". That's at 9, 15:28:56 --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Kraljevic, not Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Pardon me. Pardon me. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Susica, when there was this transport of people, from Susica to the Batkovic camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who told what to whom, can you just tell us again. Here in the transcript, it says "I saw Basic giving a list to Basic." What happened? Who gave the list to whom?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's not what it says in the statement. I don't understand English. But Veljko Basic gave the list to Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I may just interrupt you for one second. You are speaking at quite a high speed, and the interpreters might have difficulties in following you at that speed. If you speak a bit slower, then there would be no need to correct later on. But I do understand that you're not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So if I understand you correctly, your knowledge of this command structure is in part due to what you personally observed and in part due to your knowledge about how military hierarchy operated before the conflict. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, since I was a soldier myself and my father worked in the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I think it's rather than summarising the affect of the witness's evidence and what it might be, I think it's best if it comes from the witness's mouth as opposed to the summary posited by Ms. Karagiannakis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Karagiannakis, if a summary or a short repetition would create any risk of not exactly reproducing what the witness said, we would rather stick to his own words. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at paragraphs 7 to 8 of your statement. In those paragraphs, you describe local people assisting the JNA by setting up checkpoints and disarming people. Could you -- were there any other examples that you personally observed of local people assisting the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Between the 22nd and 23rd when the JNA and SDS took the town of Vlasenica, the local Serbs were already armed in the morning and they had white armbands. They had standard military equipment, and they were providing security for vital institutions like the post office, the banks, the hospital. They helped collect hunting weapons, legally-owned. They helped collect hunting rifles and pistols which were legally owned with the permission of the public security station. All those who had weapons were recorded, were on record. Those who didn't have such a record illegally possessed such weapons. They established a checkpoint by the hospital which was closest to me. And at that checkpoint, Muslims from the settlement and the pioneer division from Zeljko Lukica Street had to hand over weapons by 9.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were weapons seized from people of all ethnicities in Vlasenica Municipality or only particular ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, not from all ethnicities. Only from those of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you now look at paragraph 16 of your statement. In that paragraph you describe how local Serbs used JNA equipment to shell those villages of Pijuci, Dzamdzici, Bare, and Zaklopaca. Could you please tell me what was the ethnic makeup of these villages.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The villages of Pijuci, Dzamdzici, and Bare, and Zaklopaca were inhabited by Muslims exclusively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the populations of those villages insofar as you know do after the shelling?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Those who survived, because in Dzamdzici and Bare, there were some dead, those who survived went to Vlasenica. At least the children and the women did. Some set off in the direction of Kladanj and Zivinice, and others in the direction of Cerska. The men who were there went in the direction of Cerska illegally through the villages because they couldn't use the public roads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this statement you've described in detail the beatings and the murders that you witnessed in the four detention facilities that you were detained in. And I don't want to go into those because they are dealt with in detail in your statement. However, I'd like to ask you some additional questions just on the conditions that you experienced in those detention facilities and the nature of your fellow detainees in those facilities as far as you know. Now, first of all, you were detained in Vlasenica police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: At this stage, I would like the witness to be shown a photograph. I think...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit Number P268.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, could you take a blue -- red pen, please, it's right next to you. A blue pen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have as a rule blue for the Prosecution, black for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Yes, could you please take a blue pen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness is marking, could the document be put on the ELMO. If at least you are going to invite him to mark anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we would like to see it. Madam Usher, could you please move the ELMO in such a way that the witness...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the first place you were detained in was the Vlasenica police station. Could you please take the pen and mark that location with the number 1.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness marked a 1 on a white building in the centre of the photograph with a blue roof.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the building to the left of the photo is as we -- as you look at it is, or was in 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Under number 1, we have the police station building and the fire brigade building. That's where I marked number 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The building next to it, and there are buses in front of it. What building was that?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The building in front of which the buses is the municipal assembly of Vlasenica, and across the road we have the bank and the bus station. We have the municipal building, the bank, and the bus station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please mark the municipal building with the number 2.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the bus station with the number 3.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there is a building behind the police station which has approximately two storeys. It's not the low building directly behind the police station, but the building behind that. What was that building?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The big long building is the building of the municipal court in Vlasenica. And behind is the former municipal prison which was closed until the JNA and the SDS took power in Vlasenica, at which point it was activated and put into function in April of 1992. It's the municipal prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you mark the municipal prison with the number 4.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, going back to the conditions in the Vlasenica prison, could you please tell me the number of people detained with you in -- sorry, in the Vlasenica police station, sorry. Tell me the number of people that were on average detained with you.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the prison, in the police station, there were about 20 of us on average. The number would charge from 7 to 15, and 20 would be the maximum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the sex of the people detained there with you?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: We were all men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Karagiannakis, could you try to clarify the issue of how many people were in the police station and the prison, because I do understand that the police station is the building marked 1 whereas the prison is the building marked 4 and the witness deals with both of them in one number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's focus on the police station which is marked as number 1 on the exhibit. How many people were detained there with you?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I have just said. Up to 20 in the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you said that -- what was the sex of the people detained there?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: They were men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What the age range of the people detained there?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: From 18 to 60 years of age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know any of them personally?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I knew all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, of the people that you knew personally, were any of those people involved in any military activities?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: None of them participated in military activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of those people?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: They were all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of food were you provided with at the police station?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: We were in the police station in Vlasenica, and we received food from homes on occasion, and sometimes we wouldn't receive any. If they brought us food from homes, if there was anyone in these homes, they had to beg to obtain such food. We were hungry far more frequently than being full.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the police ever provide you with any food?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The police in the prison didn't provide us with any food, with the exception of -- apart from on one occasion when they brought us some food that had gone off. We didn't have any plates, we didn't have any spoons. They poured it into our hands. It was as if we were animals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you provided with any medical care?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the police station in Vlasenica, there wasn't any medical care of any kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe your access to water and toilet facilities.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: We could use water. We had access to water but only in the basement of the building. The person who went to get water or went to the toilet would be beaten on the way there and on the way back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, can you please describe your sleeping conditions.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Some of us slept standing, some sitting down, but there weren't any beds. There were concrete tiles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would you describe the atmosphere in the place where you were detained?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The atmosphere, in the prison? It was an atmosphere of suffering, of misery, of pain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see it's nearly time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If this would be a suitable moment for you, we'll have a break, and we'll continue at 10 minutes past 4.00. And I indicate to the parties that the Chamber is inclined to start really in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Karagiannakis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, I'd like to move on to your detention in the Vlasenica prison which you marked on the previous exhibit as number 4. Can you tell us who the commander of that prison was.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the municipal prison in Vlasenica was Sukanovic. A policeman in uniform. Some of them recognised him as a worker, an employee, of the central prison in Sarajevo. He was a professional who held this position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you treated in his presence?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the presence of the Mr. Sukanovic, the premises were aired, cleaned, it was possible to go to the toilet, to drink water. It was possible to have food brought from our homes. When he was absent, all of this was prohibited. There were beatings which did not occur in his presence. He treated us in a fair and correct manner, and as a professional policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many men were detained in that facility during your stay there?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The premises of the municipal prison consist of five cells. There were on average up to 150 of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any women or children there?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the municipal prison, there were only men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of the men that you knew personally at that prison, how many of those did you know to be involved in military activities?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, none of them were involved in such activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the people in the prison?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: They were all of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In general, what sort of food were you provided with?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: We would receive food from our homes on a daily basis, and on one occasion we were given food in the prison. The Serbs gave them this food. These were the remains that they had. Everything else boiled down to contributions from those who still had acquaintances who had remained in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe your access to water and toilet facilities.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as going to the toilet is concerned and getting water, while the warden of the prison, Sukanovic was there, that wasn't a problem. But when he was absent, we were beaten on the way to the prison and back. We would go to the prison on one occasion in the morning, and sometimes on two occasions, once in the morning and once in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This may be a translation problem, but what you said was translated back to us as, and I quote: "We would go to the prison, and on one occasion in the morning and sometimes on two occasions, once in the morning and once in the afternoon." That was in response to a question about what sort of water and toilet facilities you had. Did you mean to say prison or something else?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was referring to the use of the toilets in the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you required to do any work whilst you were at the Vlasenica prison?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the prison, in the police station, we didn't do any work, whereas in the municipal prison, we were forced to work, to loot the property of Muslims, to loot abandoned Muslim houses. We had to bury the dead in the village of Drum. We had to unload flour for the former state bakery, and we had to dig trenches at the front line in the direction of Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you take the property that you had looted from abandoned Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The items looted from abandoned Muslim houses were taken away in the Varos Street to a Muslim house that was there and was also abandoned. And it had extensive business premises in its basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who controlled those -- that house where the looted property was stored?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: People of Serbian nationality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst at the Vlasenica prison, did you have access to medical care?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the municipal prison in Vlasenica, we didn't have access to medical care given that only on one occasion two persons in white overalls came to examine us. There wasn't a physical checkup of any kind. There weren't any medicines. We just had to see them, say where it hurt, if it hurt, and then we had to return to our cells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you provided with any medications? Were you or anybody that you saw that was beaten provided with any medication?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No one was ever provided with any medication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, can you describe the sleeping conditions in that prison.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The sleeping conditions in the municipal prison consisted of the hotel in the SUP. We slept on the floor, but there was no damper. There was a parquet floor, and there were some shelves on which they used to keep certain things. We were able to use them to sleep on, whereas in the SUP prison we didn't have these facilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "SUP prison," are you referring to the police station?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on to Susica camp, can you please describe the food with which you were provided.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the Susica camp, for the first two or three days, they would bring us food from our homes, and that depended on the goodwill of the guards and of the warden. That is to say, of the commander, Dragan Nikolic, also known as Yankee. We could get food if he was in a good mood. If he wasn't, we wouldn't get any food. But subsequently, once a day we were provided with a meal brought to us by people of Serbian nationality in uniform. It was provided at about 11.00. We had about 10 plates, and as many spoons. We all had to eat from those plates. They wouldn't be washed. There was no hygiene. It was necessary to use these things to eat the food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people had to share those ten plates?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Between 500 and 550 people from the territory of three municipalities, Vlasenica, Sekovici, and Kalesija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of access did you have to drinking water?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the Susica camp, drinking water was distributed twice a day. One cup of water would be provided on each occasion. It was brought in in a military canister of about 30 litres. And they went from man to man, and one cup of water would be provided in the morning and another in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of access were you -- what sort of medical care were you given?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as medical care is concerned, no care of any kind was provided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of access did you have to toilet facilities?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as toilets were concerned, we would get up at 6 -- up until 6.15 or 6.20 at the latest. All 150 [as interpreted] of us had to run the gauntlet in order to relieve ourselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when people ran the gauntlet?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: While people ran the gauntlet, armed guards, they had the usual military automatic weapons, they were lined up to provide security of some kind in spite of the fact that those premises were encircled by a wire fence, and they kept urging everyone to hurry up. Everything had to be done as fast as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did all the people -- did all the detainees have to go to the toilet within that time period you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: They all went out during that time period, all those who were in that hangar. Anyone who needed to relieve himself went out whereas at night, they would bring us a 10-litre pot which was used as fire extinguishing equipment and 550 people used this to relieve themselves if it was necessary in the course of the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe your sleeping conditions.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as the sleeping conditions in the Susica camp, in Vlasenica is concerned, those who had arrived before me and who were taken from their homes had some sort of a blanket. Some people had a sort of sponge in order to sleep on. And I and people from Kalesija and Sekovici slept on concrete.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you forced to do any work while you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell us what that was.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Repair work to a road from Vlasenica in the direction of the Susica camp. There was also the cleaning of Jusuf Dautovic's flat. This person was of Muslim nationality, and it was -- involved transporting his property in the vicinity of the Susica camp. Those items were set on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were those items set on fire?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know why they were burnt, but when we were unloading the items from the ATC vehicle. We were given a jerry can with petrol in it and we were given a lighter to set fire to these things. And they said "you will set fire to them, not the Serbs."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any choice as to whether you did the work that you were asked to do?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: If you refused to do what they asked the detainees to do, you could be beaten. And we all feared for our lives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the sex of the people detained at Susica?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: There were six to seven women, one of them was about 80 years old. They were in the Susica camp. Most of the detainees were Muslims. They were men. They were adults from the municipalities of Kalesija, Sekovici, and Vlasenica, and there were some young men who were returning from their regular military service in the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of the men that you personally knew in Susica camp, how many of those were involved in military activities?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the territory of Vlasenica Municipality, in the territory of the town of Vlasenica, there was no military activity. Those people who were in the Susica camp and whom I personally know, as far as I know, none of them participated in a conflict of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown the next photographic exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have we dealt with the previous one, Ms. Karagiannakis?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Yes, we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because very often, the Registrar copies the short description, and it says "aerial photo of Susica camp." But I haven't heard anything about the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: The previous one is an aerial photograph of Vlasenica town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but it's on your list indicated as Susica camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: I'll seek to correct that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's Vlasenica town. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit Number P269.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just describe what that picture depicts.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The picture depicts Vlasenica, the suburbs of Vlasenica. The road that we maintained leading towards the Susica camp to big barracks and one small barrack, the latter was not used while I was in the camp. And in the larger frame, we can see the camp, the hangar where people were Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond accommodated. You can also see a smaller camp with the MTS, the materiel and equipment. You can also see the sentry, and you can also see a house in which women and children were, those who were brought to the Susica camp. You can also see the place where Mr. Jusuf Dautovic's things were set on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you mark with the number 1 the place where people were detained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The picture on the ELMO is not very clear. Could the light be or... Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you mark with the number 2 where the sentry post was.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see you've marked two positions as sentry posts. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the entrance gate and another sentry post where guards would be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you mark with the number 3 the place where the women were detained.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you mark with the number 4 the town of Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you estimate the distance between Vlasenica town and Susica camp, please.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The distance between Vlasenica and the Susica camp is approximately a kilometre and a half to 2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I've finished with that exhibit. Now, Mr. Osmanovic, I'd like to move on to the -- your detention in Batkovic camp. In which municipality is Batkovic camp, prison?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
