utterances.text: The Batkovic camp is 12 kilometres from Bijeljina towards the Sava River in the complex of the so-called Agrosemberija, the former wheat hangars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did the detainees that were in Batkovic camp with you come from?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The detainees who were in the Batkovic camp, the first group which was transported from the Susica camp; the second group was transported from the Susica camp and were told that they would be exchanged. Still we found them in the Batkovic camp. After that, they started bringing people from Zvornik, Lopari, Ugljevik, Bijeljina, Rogatica, and even 512 people from Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people arrived with you to Batkovic from Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Together with me, some 400 people came from the Susica camp and their transportation took approximately three days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people arrived from Manjaca? Pardon me. Sorry, you've answered that question. When did the people who arrived from Manjaca arrive at Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: They arrived after the Manjaca camp was dismantled. Actually one day before it would be dismantled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the approximate date?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the date. I believe it was in 1993. At the beginning of 1993 or the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Of the people that were with you in 1992 at Batkovic, can you please tell me what sex those detainees had -- were.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the Batkovic camp, there were two women from Rogatica. And the rest were men, and there were some children aged 16 who didn't want to be separated from their fathers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of those detainees?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: From Vlasenica, Kalesija, Sekovici, Zvornik, and Bijeljina, those people were of Muslim ethnicity, whereas from Brcko some people who arrived were also Croats. There were only Muslims and Croats in that camp. Later on, they brought four Albanians who had worked as bakers somewhere around Doboj. So finally, we ended up with some Albanians in that camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the people that you personally knew at that camp, how many of those people were engaged in military activities before detention?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: All those who arrived with me and whom I knew, none of them participated in any military activities. Later on, one person was brought to Batkovic camp. His name was Nedim Mostarcevic. He was from Tuzla. He was brought wounded and we were told that he had been captured on the front line. After him, they also brought a man from the territory of my municipality. His name was Fadil Alihodzic. He was also charged with being a member of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to the conditions in the camp. What sort of food were you provided with?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: When we arrived in the Batkovic camp, we received a loaf of bread for breakfast, and it had to be cut to 12 or 15 slices, and one egg. That was our breakfast. For lunch, we would receive some cooked food. And in the evening, we would get boiled corn flour. What we received the first day was exactly the amount that we received on the day when the camp was filled to its capacity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you clarify something, please. How much bread did you receive for breakfast for each person?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Per person, one slice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of access did you have to water?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: There was water. There were five or six pipes, and we could use water throughout the day. We had access to water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What access did you have to toilet facilities?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the Batkovic camp, we were allowed to use toilet during the day, not during the night. And we had a makeshift toilet. It was a hole that was dug out 10 metres long, 1 and a half metres wide, and 50 centimetres deep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe your sleeping conditions.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the Batkovic camp, there were two persons sharing a military mattress, and a military mattress consists of three parts. And the size of it is 1 square metre, and this had to be shared by two people. After that, they removed those mattresses from us, and we had to sleep on straw, on hay. This is what we used to sleep on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you required to do any labour?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: We had to work every day. We had to go to Agrosemberija to work in the fields. We work on constructing an airport at the exit from Bijeljina. We also worked on the front line. We had to bury the dead. We had to do the felling, various transports, whatever the people who were on the front line couldn't do. On their behalf, the detainees had to do instead of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do on the front lines?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: On the front lines, we had to dig trenches for the Serbian army. We also carried ammunition for the Serbian army to the areas which were not accessible to vehicles. We also had to do felling for the Serbian army so they didn't have to do that. We also built kilns for the dugouts where they were located. Whatever their men used to do in the past, we had to do instead of them. We also had to clean the streets in the town. We did all sorts of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were working on the front lines, was combat ongoing?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: On two occasions while combat was ongoing. One time in the vicinity of Lopari. That's when a young man from Divic was killed. That was on the 5th of December 2002. And the second time, again, in the vicinity of Lopari towards Celic village, we had two wounded and two dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, you mentioned the date 5 December 2002. Did you mean 2002 when you said it?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I apologise. It was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If you didn't want to do the work that was asked of you, were you able to refuse?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the Batkovic camp, you were not allowed to refuse to go to work. There were group leaders who conducted people to looting in Ahmici or to other Muslim villages. We were also taken to the front lines. This person who was the group leader would just count people. They would be loaded onto lorries and they would be taken to the designated places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the village of Ahmici. Which municipality are you -- in which municipality is that Ahmici village?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Village -- Akmadzici is on the Bijeljina-Ugljevik road and it is in the Municipality of Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your statement dated October 1994, you name -- you identify by name a number of victims of killings and beatings in these detention facilities. What is the ethnicity of the people that you have identified by name?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Those people whom I named --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... I think for the sake of the transcript it would be useful to have the paragraph number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: These names appear all the way through the statement. But I can -- basically, they are in nearly every paragraph. I can identify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to be practical. Did the witness testify about the ethnicity of those who were kept in Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the question would be, well, let's -- I do not imagine that any of the victims of these acts were those in charge of the camp, but were those who were detained. So isn't it sufficiently then established, at least on the basis of this testimony, what was the ethnicity of those who were considered to be victims?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. I was suggesting for the sake of the transcript it would be useful to nominate the specific paragraphs because we are dealing with a statement that is -- that has 70 paragraphs. And not all of them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but I think the matter as such is not really an issue. On the basis of the earlier testimony and -- let me ask you, Mr. Osmanovic, whenever you are talking about -- whenever you mentioned any name of a victim in Batkovic camp, what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were Croats as well. But those that I knew and that I was acquainted with were all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And those you mentioned by name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, could you please look at paragraph 9 of your statement, paragraphs 9 and 7 of your statement. You named a number of people who were assisting the JNA in the takeover. What was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraphs 7 and 9, I mentioned Dragan Bastah, also known as Car, Dragisa Milakovic, he was Bastah's neighbour. These people were of Serbian ethnic origin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 11, you mention two names. Can you please tell me what their ethnicity was.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 11, I mention Rajko Ninic who worked in the 10th August of Vlasenica -- the furniture company and also Mane Djuric who at the time was the chief of the police station. Before the occupation, Mane Djuric was an anti-fire protection inspector. And they are both Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 14, you mentioned a number of people that were involved in your initial arrest. Could you please tell me what their ethnicity was.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: People mentioned in paragraph 14 are also Serbs. Stevo Mumovic hailed from a different municipality, from Han Pijesak. The others hailed from the territory of Vlasenica Municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 17, you mention a number of people that were involved in your initial long-term arrest and detention at the police station. What was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: All these people mentioned in paragraph 17 are Serbs. At the bottom of this paragraph, people mentioned there are my neighbours from my neighbourhood. That's how I knew the names of their parents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mention some special military police in the following paragraph, 18, that were involved in beatings. What was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: People mentioned in paragraph 18 are also Serbs. They differed from others because they wore camouflage uniforms. They were allowed to enter the police station, the prison, and the Susica camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity insofar as you know of the guards and other official personnel at the Vlasenica police station?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: They were all Serbs. The employees of Muslim origin who worked until the day the JNA entered Vlasenica lost their jobs. They were dismissed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity insofar as you know personally of the guards and other official personnel at the Vlasenica prison, municipal prison?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Also Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity insofar as you know of the guards and other official personnel at Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: They were all Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the ethnicity insofar as you know of the guards and other officials at Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In Batkovic, also Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you know and learned subsequently, how many Muslims remained in Vlasenica town at the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992 when I left, in the Susica camp there were about 150 people of Muslim origin. And there were some who had remained in their houses. They were still there because Serbs had not taken them to the prison. Currently, the municipal commission of Vlasenica Municipality is still searching for some 1400 people from the territory of Vlasenica Municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people remained voluntarily and freely as at the end of 1992, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Voluntarily, nobody would have stayed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Of course, just an objection in relation to the value of the evidence. Of course, he was, on his own evidence, at the end of 1992 not at liberty. So it's doubtful as to what value that sort of evidence might be for the Tribunal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question started "as far as you know and learned subsequently," and of course if the witness did not count the remaining Muslim population of Vlasenica, then of course the source of knowledge muse be a different one and should be evaluated. It is a matter that could have been dealt with in cross-examination as well or at any later stage. Please proceed, Ms. Karagiannakis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just have one final question for you, Mr. Osmanovic. Can you please describe what happened to your family after the takeover of Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: After the takeover of Vlasenica, my older brother, whose wife was a Serb and he lived in the Piskavice neighbourhood, he was in house arrest, and he was killed on the 22nd of September 1992. My mother, my two sisters, and my younger brother were also detained in the Susica camp. From that camp, my mother was able to leave together with my older sister towards Srpska. My younger sister and my younger brother stayed there. The whereabouts of my younger brother are not known, and my sister from Susica went to the Pelemis camp. An exhumation was carried out a few days ago and it was established that all of the bodies there had burned down. Only the two of us still remain of my entire family unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: That concludes my examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Karagiannakis. Ms. Loukas, are you ready at least to start to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would indicate as I indicated prior to the witness coming in, of course, I've received additional information from the Prosecution today. I think it might be useful in the circumstances, we could take an early break. There's some material I need to obtain from Ms. Philpott. And then I'm happy to commence my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Philpott is clear what Ms. Loukas expects you to give her? Yes, okay. I'm just looking at the clock. Ms. Loukas, if we would have a break now, the second break usually is 20 minutes. Then we would have one hour and three quarters left, which is just a bit too much for one tape. If you could make, perhaps, a start, if it were only for 10 or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm happy to do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we would still have an early break, but not as early as you...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm happy to do that, Your Honour. I'll just need the lectern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, Ms. Loukas, counsel for the Defence, will now examine you, but we'll soon have a break. Then she'll continue after the break. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Ms. Loukas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Osmanovic.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Osmanovic, I don't propose to take you through any of the unfortunate and tragic circumstances you have been through. What I will be doing is asking you a series of questions that hopefully most of which can be answered with yes or no. Are you with me?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, first of all, Mr. Osmanovic, I think in your statement right at the beginning, you indicate that - and this is your statement of 1994 that I think you have before you - and in about paragraph 2, you deal with the fact, sort of historical background material in relation to August 1991. Do you see where I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you talk there about the sort of -- the Serb nationalistic songs and that sort of background. And continuing in paragraph 3, of the communities beginning to sort of divide amongst themselves. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course, that was at the time you're dealing with there, that was, of course, in the context of the background of the war that was going on in Croatia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, going on to the issue of uniforms and military service, you, of course, as did all men in the former Yugoslavia of an appropriate age, you had to serve compulsory military service. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was when I was 18.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course, when you did your military service, you were given a uniform?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: While I was serving in the army, I was given a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course, it was generally known at that time, of course, throughout Yugoslavia that all people who had served their military service and were reservists had JNA uniforms. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, it's not correct. Those who had served compulsory service became reservists, but they did not all have JNA uniforms. Those who had a war assignment in another unit, in a different unit, such as was my case. I was a member of a fire brigade. I had a firefighters' uniform, not a military uniform. Those who were assigned to the maintenance of some facilities in utility companies also didn't have military uniforms. They worked in overalls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm not trying to confuse you here, Mr. Osmanovic. So what I'll do is just take you back to some previous testimony you gave when you gave evidence in the trial against Mr. Milosevic, okay? I think you nodded your head, but for the transcript it's important that you actually say "yes" or "da" as opposed to --

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, for the benefit of the Court, I'm dealing with the cross-examination at page 29.504 of the transcript for the benefit of the Court and counsel. Now, of course, when you gave evidence on that occasion, you were again subject to the oath just as you are today. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told, of course, the truth on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to confirm some answers you gave there in relation to questions. The first question is "in relation to uniforms, you did your military service, didn't you, and you had the same JNA uniform. Right?" And your response was -- answer -- your answer was "yes." Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: That had to do with doing my military service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed. I'm just getting you to confirm your answers from the previous trial. Now, the next question you were asked was this: "Wasn't it a generally known fact throughout Yugoslavia that all reservists had JNA uniforms?" And your answer was "yes." Correct? Agreed?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for the reservists who were part of or with the reserve force of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And further, you were asked this question: "So these who were on the police force or on the reserve force, they all had these JNA uniforms. They all wore JNA uniforms that were available to them all that time even before the conflicts broke out. Is that right?" And your answer was "yes."

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: This has to do with the reserve police force, and they had their own uniforms. The police force had different uniforms. And this is now about the beginning of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Those who didn't have the uniforms of the reserve police, those who didn't have some other kind of uniform, those who didn't have the olive-drab uniform of the JNA, they put those uniforms on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But in any event, you agree, of course, here today with the answers that you gave on a previous occasion. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course, the situation is that to your knowledge, of course, there were a significant number of people who had uniforms throughout the former Yugoslavia, prior to the breakout of the war?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were quite a few people who had uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's quite apart from, of course, people who were then currently serving in the army. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, going on to another point, I just want to take you to your statement, again the statement that's in evidence and you have before you. And that's at, if you'd like to turn to paragraph 5 of your statement. Do you have that before you?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicate there that "everything was calm - indicating in Vlasenica - until the 23rd or 24th of April when the JNA came in to town." Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I stated in that paragraph that up until the arrival of the JNA, it was calm in the town, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think the situation is that when the JNA arrived, you did not see them abuse or mistreat anyone. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, introducing a curfew also amounts to maltreating people. Entering houses, keeping people in their houses is also maltreating people. The JNA when they proclaimed together with the crisis staff that arms should be handed over, they guaranteed full security, full safety for people of Muslim nationality. Unfortunately, those who remained and believed the army, such as was my case, they experienced these things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Again, Mr. Osmanovic I'm not trying to confuse you in any way. What I'll do is I'll just get you to confirm a question and answer that you gave when you were being cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic. Are you with me?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm following you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You were asked this question: "When I asked you this, when they arrived, when this JNA unit arrived whose size we cannot identify, did they mistreat or abuse anyone"?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, could counsel indicate where their --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The page number.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Certainly. It's page 29478 for the benefit of the Court and the Prosecution. Sometimes I get a little ahead of myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your response was: "Apart from walking about town, I did not see them do anything like abuse or mistreat anyone." I take it you agree with the response you gave in relation to this particular issue when you were giving evidence in the trial against Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I agree with everything that I stated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to Mr. Nikolic, now, to your knowledge, of course, Mr. Nikolic was, of course, a -- someone that you knew from before the war. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew Dragan Nikolic before the war, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you knew him before the war as a local Serb. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think prior to the war, he was a civilian employee at the Alpro enterprise. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the factory for these aluminum products.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also, I think that when you were finally released from Batkovic, you were exchanged for Serb civilians. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was exchanged when there were other civilians of Serbian nationality who were going over to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think that this may be an appropriate time and will leave us enough tape for the rest of the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It certainly does. Thank you, Ms. Loukas. We'll adjourn until 5.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Osmanovic, just prior to the break, we were talking to you about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your microphone, Ms. Loukas. If you use your headphones, you'll hear that your microphone should be switched on.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I thought it was, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the beginning it wasn't. Please, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, now, Mr. Osmanovic, just prior to the break, we were dealing with paragraph 5 of your statement in relation to the fact that everything was calm until the 23rd or 24th of April when the JNA came into town. You recall that, of course?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to that, of course, so prior to the JNA arriving, there weren't a lot of armed forces around, were there?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the territory of the Municipality of Vlasenica, Your Honours, there was no JNA garrison with the exception of Han Pijesak 18 kilometres away. There was the military post 1524 there, and I saw a group of JNA members in Vlasenica. They were in Tisca and Milici. That's where they were located. Those municipalities in the vicinity of Vlasenica. And there were military vehicles that were located there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But prior to the JNA arriving, you didn't see any tanks, did you?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course, there were no threats from the SDS or anybody else prior to the JNA arriving, were there?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, there were no threats in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you didn't notice a lot of armed people carrying arms or anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the Panorama Hotel, I noticed people who came there and they were armed and were in uniform. They would sit down there, but they did not act in a provocative way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the only place that you saw armed people was at the Panorama Hotel prior to the arrival of the JNA. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before the JNA arrived in town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there was, of course, no shooting during the day and that sort of thing prior to the arrival of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: There was no shooting in the town before the arrival of the JNA. When the JNA arrived, there was no shooting in the town either apart from a few shots that were fired from the vicinity of an elevation, a hill above Vlasenica. The shots were fired in the direction of the settlement, and the person in charge of the SDS in Vlasenica was asked why there was shooting from above. He said that the army was there to secure peace and that there wouldn't be any problems and they would look into the affair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd also asked you a question just before the break in relation to Dragan Nikolic, and you indicated that of course you knew him prior to the war as a local Serb and what his previous employment had been. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the time that you saw him in Susica, he, I take it, wore a camouflage uniform. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I saw Dragan Nikolic on one other occasion before I arrived in Susica. He was in front of the Crisis Staff and armed with an automatic rifle. He was wearing a camouflage uniform. But when I arrived in Susica camp, I saw Dragan Nikolic was armed with an automatic rifle, a pistol, a knife, and hand grenades. He was in camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to take you to paragraph 13 of your statement. If you can just open up your statement there at paragraph 13, that's the statement of October 1994.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicate there that you had Muslim friends at the bauxite company, and they told you they did not receive their monthly salary in May 1992. And you indicate there that your brother was working there and did not get paid. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your friends and your brother were still working at the bauxite company in May, of course?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: They worked in the Alpro factory which is part of the bauxite mine in Vlasenica. That's one company that consisted of a number of departments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But of course, Muslims were still employed in Vlasenica in May. That's what I'm just asking you to confirm.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Some of the Muslims who had remained were working because work obligation had been introduced by the crisis staff of the Serbian Municipality of Vlasenica. And whoever failed to go to work would lose their job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Osmanovic, I want to take you to paragraph 64 of your statement. Thank you. And I think that you were asked some questions in relation to paragraph 64 earlier today by Ms. Karagiannakis. You recall being asked those questions?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I do recall it, and I think that I answered those questions, the questions that Ms. Karagiannakis asked me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicate in your statement there that you're of the belief that Mr. Milomir Stanic was in charge of all civil and military departments in Vlasenica. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that is correct because you could see his signature on all the information reports, or rather orders from the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the basis for your belief is seeing his signature on orders from the Crisis Staff. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were shown a document earlier today. That's potential exhibit P267.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: If the witness might be shown that document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think in your evidence you indicated that that was similar or identical to the document that you received. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this has to do with permission to move freely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed. Now, of course, the exhibit in question in front of you is not signed, of course, by Mr. Stanic, is it?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: This document was signed on behalf of Milenko Stanic, somebody called R. Matic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that similar in relation to the document that you had, or didn't you notice?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Asked and answered. I asked him that question in examination-in-chief. He said it was signed by Stanic, the one that he had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, the witness answered that question, so I wonder, you more or less put it to him as if he had not noticed something or where he was clear in his answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm happy to rephrase the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Osmanovic, I don't suppose at the time you paid a great deal of attention to whether or not it was signed by Mr. Stanic or somebody else on behalf of him. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that question. The witness was asked who signed it. He clearly stated it was signed by Stanic. I don't see...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that's not the question at this moment, Ms. Karagiannakis. Mr. Osmanovic, the question to you is whether at that time looking at these kind of documents whether you paid any specific attention to whether Mr. Stanic signed it or -- the question was whether that was correct, whether you would not have paid much attention to it at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't pay so much attention to the signature. It was a standard form, and the name of the person who applied for the pass was added in handwriting. All the passes bore original stamps, and it was typewritten "Crisis Staff, Milenko Stanic" on every pass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just also in relation to that material you have contained in paragraph 64 of your statement, I think you indicated in response to a Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond question from Ms. Karagiannakis that your belief that Mr. Stanic was in charge of all civil and military departments in Vlasenica was, of course, based on your observation of this document and another document that you saw when you went to work, and also on the basis of your own understanding of hierarchy. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, going to paragraph 65 of your statement, you were again asked questions about this earlier today. And what you've indicated in paragraph 65 is that in that second sentence there "that the crisis committee appeared to make all the final decisions in town." Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, part of your -- that again is your belief. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is my personal belief for the following reason: Without the pass being issued by the crisis staff, you couldn't leave the town. You couldn't move about the town without that pass. The Crisis Staff also introduced the curfew. It introduced the order on the delivery of timber from the furniture factory without any other documents. And based on all this, I conclude that the Crisis Staff was in charge of everything in the town, that it had all the power in the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So it's your belief. You based it on -- it's your belief. Correct, yes?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is my belief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's your personal belief.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: My personal belief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've based it on a number of things, including, one, the appearance of Mr. Stanic's name on orders you'd seen that you've given evidence of in your evidence in chief. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also that you saw his name on an order in relation to the 10 August company asking the company to give the army wooden boards. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also on the basis of the order in relation to the curfew. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to that, I think you also indicated that your basis for this -- for these beliefs that you have is that the background of the plebiscite in relation to the various Serb autonomous areas. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also in relation to what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, why don't you come to your point. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also in relation to what you saw on TV and newspapers. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is the basis for your personal beliefs that you've expressed in paragraphs 64 and 65. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's move to paragraph 70 of your statement. Now, I think you indicate there a gentleman by the name of Kraljevic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: His family name was Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. What was his first name?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what his first name was. I know his family name was Kraljevic. His sister, Malina, went to school with me, and he was born in Malina village in Vlasenica Municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event, you've indicated there that - and I think the background to this is that Nikolic indicated in Susica that he was God and the law. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: He stated that he was the God and the law as far as the Susica camp was concerned. However, when Kraljevic was supposed to come, he came in a vehicle owned by Mustafa Jasarevic who had disappeared. Nikolic told us, hurry up, clean the premises, the king is coming, the commander is coming. The major who had arrived to inform people during a briefing that there would be an exchange of people from Vlasenica, Kalesija, and Sekovici, Nikolic told him "I am the God and the law here, but Kralj - or the king - is somebody I report to and I obey only him." When Veljko Basic, the retired policeman came, he gave Nikolic a list. The latter told him that Kralj was his commander. When Kraljevic arrived in the camp, Kraljevic saluted, and Veljko Basic -- it was always the case that a lower ranking officer would salute the higher ranking officer. I'm talking about the military customs here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you're speaking about your understanding of military customs from your experience when you were in the JNA serving your compulsory service. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Based on my knowledge and experience, I wouldn't say. It has nothing to do with my knowledge and experience. I'm talking about the rules of service in the JNA. Before I served in the JNA and while I served in the JNA, it is the lower rank that salutes the higher rank, and then the higher rank, if they wish to do so, can salute back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on to another topic, Mr. Osmanovic, on the 22nd of May, when you were arrested, you were asked questions. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Sorry. Could counsel please indicate whether counsel is referring to the statement at this point?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you were arrested, Mr. Osmanovic, on the 22nd of May, you were asked - 1992 - you were asked questions. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what kind of questions were you asked?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: From the moment I was taken out of my house from where I was taken, I was asked a few questions. They were looking for Hasan Dzindo, an SDA activist. I couldn't answer any of those questions. On the following day, they started interrogating me at the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they asked you things, like, for example, who are Muslims. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was asked about certain members of the SDA. Since I was not a member of that party, I couldn't answer them. They also asked me about weapons. They asked me about a gun, and a gun is not a toy. You can't hide it. It is a big artillery piece, isn't it? They also asked me about mixed patrols and whether those people were armed or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And they asked you who armed the Muslims. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: They asked me if I knew whether anybody had illegal weapons. And they also asked me about a good friend of mine, Mensur Smajic who had surrendered his automatic rifle. They asked me whether I knew where he got that weapon from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Osmanovic, I'm not trying to confuse you here. I'll just refer you back to some answers you gave when you were giving evidence in relation to the proceedings against Mr. Nikolic. The page reference is page 253 of the proceedings in relation to Mr. Nikolic for the benefit of the Court and counsel. And you were asked by the Presiding Judge, in fact, "what were the questions they put to you?" "What questions did they ask you?" And your response was: "The questions they asked me were who armed the Muslims, who prepared the uprising against Serbs, where is the cannon, do I know of my neighbour Mensur Smajic, or the people who were active in the Muslim party?" Now, do you remember that question from the Presiding Judge when you gave evidence in the proceedings against Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: It was in 1995, and I believe that I have answered those questions again today. They asked me about the cannon. They asked me about Mensur Smajic, about some people from the party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And they asked you about who armed the Muslims and who prepared the uprising against Serbs. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think -- and of course, you also gave evidence in relation to the proceedings against Mr. Tadic as well. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the people that you've referred to at, for example, Batkovic camp, were any of them wearing hats or caps?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived at the Batkovic camp, from the Susica camp to the Batkovic camp, we were escorted by men in camouflage hats. In the Batkovic camp, only Vojo wore a cap, and he wore insignia on the cap. When we went to dig trenches, there were people there in olive-drab uniforms and a Serbian flag on their hats. I also came across people who wore head covers with crosses on them. I also came across people with some eagle signs with the insignia of Draza Mihajlovic, that is to say, cockades. There were different insignia there then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just in relation to Batkovic, the men in uniform that you've referred to in Batkovic camp were all bare-headed. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: All but Vojo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just going to some background material in relation to Vlasenica, Mr. Osmanovic, were you aware of in September 1991 of mixed Croat-Muslim paramilitary groups setting out stakeouts and frisking travellers on the road between Milici and the bauxite mine?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not. Now, how about in February of 1992, were you aware of paramilitary formations of Muslims and Croats kidnapping people and hijacking trucks and conducting searches on the road between Milici and the bauxite mine?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Madam. In the territory of Vlasenica, there were only two Croats whom I know. One was a waiter, and the other was a police officer. They lived in mixed marriages. Their wives were Serbs. In Vlasenica Municipality, there were only Serbs and Muslims. In Vlasenica Municipality, we did not have any Croat inhabitants. I don't know what Croats or formations composed of Croats and Muslims are you referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Osmanovic, just listen carefully to my question because my question didn't imply that the Croats were from Vlasenica. There are Croats who don't live in Vlasenica. So all I need is a response to the question I asked you.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard nothing of those.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you have any information in relation to around about 16th of May 1992 the disarming of Muslim paramilitary formations in Zaklopaca?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Paramilitary formations in Zaklopaca, if women, children, and elderly men are paramilitary, I don't know. I've never seen a woman or a child carrying arms. You can read in the reports of the commission for Srdj that has recently excavated 80 bodies of women, children, and elderly men, the entire village of Zaklopaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, I'd like to give you the following direction. The only question that was asked of you, whether you have any information in relation to disarming of Muslim paramilitary formations in Zaklopaca on the 16th of May. If you don't have such information, just say "no, I don't know."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you don't know anything about other groups or other persons that would have been disarmed on the 16th of May in that village, then of course you can say, well, I didn't know of any paramilitary formations. But I know that, and then you tell us what you know. But you are -- your response goes far beyond what was asked. And I'd like you very much to focus and concentrate on the questions put to you. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you aware on the 21st of May or have you any information in regard to on the 21st of May on the road between Milici and Rudnik in the village of Zutica of Muslims killing eight civilians including two women and a child?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, whilst you were in Susica camp, were you aware of Muslim fighters who were kept there?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were only civilians in the Susica camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: I was just going to say asked and answered. He was asked of the people that he knew at Susica camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One of the disadvantages of examining a witness -- witnesses through translation is that it's not easy to object immediately. I think, Ms. Karagiannakis, that a similar answer has been given now, so let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you tell the Court that you weren't personally aware of any Muslim fighters being held in Susica camp. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was not aware of any fighters that were in Susica camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to everyone in Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I spoke to the people I knew and with whom I could speak. I couldn't speak to people from Kalesija because I didn't know them. I couldn't speak to people from Sekovici because I didn't know them either. However, I could and I did speak to people from Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you aware of any paramilitaries, Muslim paramilitaries, in Vlasenica in late March or in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of any Muslim paramilitary organisations in Vlasenica during that period of time. However, there was a checkpoint which was erected by villagers of Drum in the Muslim cemetery of Vlasenica. Whether they were armed or not, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Osmanovic, just in relation to paragraph 16 of your statement, you've indicated that the JNA left all their equipment. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you're not in a position, of course, to know whether or not in the entire Municipality of Vlasenica that the entirety of the JNA equipment was left there, are you?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was not in a position to know that. However, the tanks and the armoured people carriers were parked by the playground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So to your knowledge, as far as you're concerned, it may be the case that the JNA did take a significant proportion of their equipment with them. Do you agree with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I would not agree with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Osmanovic, two of your statements have been tendered today in evidence. But there is, of course, a third statement which you gave on the 11th of October 1995. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'll just arrange to have a copy of the B/C/S version placed before you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Of course, the Prosecution have their own copies, Your Honour, but I have copies of the English version for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Loukas. May I ask the Prosecution, the Chamber was in the assumption that we would receive the statements, the previous statements by witnesses, and I also indicated that the Chamber would read them in order to be better able to control the examinations. Now, I see that this is a statement which I do not remember having received.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, you're quite right. But I only saw that instruction from the Chamber this day. And in the course of preparation, I understand the instruction was given tomorrow we will seek -- yesterday, sorry, we will seek to seek to comply with that in future. But it somehow missed this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you still could have delivered it this morning. Let's proceed, and I do understand it's a transitional problem. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have that statement before you, the third statement, Mr. Osmanovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just in relation to that statement, of course, the -- what you have there is true, accurate, to the best of your ability, of course, and signed as such?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you indicate that there were three Muslim prisoners in Batkovic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: We were all Muslims, and there were some Croats. The three who were involved in the beatings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these particular Muslims that you refer to in your statement were involved in beating other Muslims. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, I think one of the prisoners you referred to, Fikret Smajlovic wore a uniform.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: There were two wearing a uniform, Fikret Smajlovic, known Piklic from Brezovo Polje, and Esad Bekric, known as the Policeman

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they both wore uniforms. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think it's the case that Mr. Smajlovic also had a car that he had access to. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: He had a red Jugo 45.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: If I might have a moment, Your Honour. I'm just looking for a document. It's a problem, Your Honours, I think with having too many papers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to what I was asking you about in relation to these Muslim detainees who were also beating the Muslims and two of whom had uniforms and one of whom had a car, I think you've also indicated something in relation to these gentlemen in paragraph 60 of your statement. And you indicate that they appeared to be more violent than the Chetnik guards. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, especially the first two. Fikret Smajlovic, called Piklic, and Zahirovic Dzemal, known as Spajzer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just in relation to the situation there with these guards, with these detainees, would you agree with me, Mr. Osmanovic, that it seems to have been something of a chaotic situation at that camp?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't just chaotic, it was more than chaotic.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Loukas. Ms. Karagiannakis, is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Just two questions arising out of the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Re-examined by Ms. Karagiannakis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, when you were questioned in the Nikolic Rule 61 hearing, the Defence counsel recounted the Presiding Judge's questions to you when you were arrested -- after you were arrested on the 22nd of May and when you were interrogated, and you were asked about elements of Muslim resistance. Do you recall your answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember my answer to that question. I could tell you in part that I couldn't answer the questions because I didn't know where those people were. I wasn't a member of the SDA, and those are the people they accused. They asked me about those people, and I didn't know about their whereabouts. So I couldn't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of any Muslim resistance at all?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of any kind of Muslim resistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now, in relation to the three Muslims who were beating people at Batkovic camp, how was it that they were able to do this or why were they doing this?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Fikret Smajlovic, a.k.a. Piklic, was taken there with a group of people from Brezovo Polje. According to what they themselves said, they were providing security for the Sava to prevent the Croats from entering Bosna. As soon as he arrived, he started issuing orders. He ordered people to go and have breakfast or lunch, he ordered us to get up at a certain time and ordered people to go to work. He could move around freely both within and outside the camp. If anyone had any money on them - those who had money had German marks - they could only exchange these German marks with them. If they found out they were exchanging those marks with someone else in order to obtain cigarettes, that money would be taken from them. Zahirovic Dzemal was in the Susica camp in Vlasenica. He came to the Batkovic camp, and when I arrived he was in charge of a group that was working in the camp, that was fencing in the camp. He beat those people with a baton, and Hidovic used more primitive means. Chairs, sticks, wood, et cetera. Whereas Bekric Esad, known as the Policajac, was brought there with a group of prisoners. He was in a column of soldiers from Tuzla. He was taken to Bijeljina. No one beat him. And he together with Piklic and Spajzer took out a group of so-called specials, special men. That's the name that they gave to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just ask you, were the guards aware of the activities of these individuals?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they do about these activities?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing. They just laughed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Karagiannakis.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I have no further questions to ask on the basis of the questions that were just asked, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions. Judge El Mahdi has one or more questions for you. Questioned by the Court: JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Witness, I have two minor questions I would like to put to you. My first question is about Mr. Sukanovic. As far as you are aware, was he part of the SDS party? Was he a member?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: With regard to Mr. Sukanovic, Your Honour, I don't know whether he was an SDS member. The first time I saw him was in the Vlasenica municipal prison. The second time he brought a group of prisoners from the municipal prison, from the Susica camp, and he was recognised by Danijel Mujkanovic there. And he told me, not just me, but to everyone, but he knew that man and he had been in the central prison in Sarajevo where he worked as a professional policeman. As to whether he was an SDS member, I do not know. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Perhaps this is a matter of general knowledge that the key posts were shared between the parties. Was the post of chief of police one that was given to the SDS party? Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: At the first multiparty elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Your Honour, that is to say, in Vlasenica Municipality, the post of chief of police went to the SDS party. The post of police commander went to the Muslims. The late Fadil Turkovic held that post. Whereas the prison to which Sukanovic came -- JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] What post did Mr. Sukanovic have?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: He wasn't in Vlasenica at all. The municipal prison didn't exist until the SDS came to power and until the JNA arrived in the town. It wasn't in function. The municipal prison was put into function when these authorities arrived. He came from the other side. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] So he was appointed in a certain sense by the SDS party. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: He was appointed by someone. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Who held power, though?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The crisis staff did. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And the crisis staff belonged to whom?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: To the Serbian Municipality of Vlasenica. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] In other words, it was the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I've got a few questions for you as well. First question is you told us that 512 prisoners in Batkovic arrived from Manjaca camp. How do you know exactly that these were 512 and not approximately 500 or 511 or 513? What --

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Because, Your Honour, two brothers distributed food to them, and they were in a separate hangar. They had to count -- or they must have counted 512 of them in Hangar Number 12 in Batkovic. They came from Manjaca. They were provided with food. And I knew about this because this is what the men who distributed food to them said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then another question is about the crisis staff or crisis committee. Do you know anything about when it was established?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the date of its establishment. But according to the news, the television, the newspapers, and the radio, there was information about the formation of the Autonomous Region of Birac and the Serbian Municipality of Vlasenica with his headquarters in Milici. As to when the crisis staff was formed, I don't know. But when the JNA arrived and when the power was taken over by SDS members, there was a crisis staff in the Municipality of Vlasenica and it had its headquarters in the bauxite mine in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you do not know whether it was there before already, although perhaps invisible at that time for you?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't know how it was established? By whom? Under what authority?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. But the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Vlasenica couldn't have been founded by the Muslims, Your Honour, not if it was called the "Serbian" Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So your knowledge is -- or at least, you assume on the basis of your knowledge that it was Serb-organised, but you don't have any further details?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have no further questions for you. Do the parties have any further questions triggered by the questions put to the witness by the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it does not trigger any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Osmanovic, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you for coming. It's a long distance to The Hague. You've answered the questions of both parties and of the Bench. I'd like to thank you for that because it's important for this Chamber to hear the evidence of those who have been present during that time in the relevant places. I'd like to wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, you may escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I would like to pay some attention to the exhibits presented during the last few days, but there are still a few outstanding issues which I would like to hear about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. First, with respect to the intercept to which the Court drew our attention the other day, as I think the Court suspected, and certainly as I suspected at the time, it was a formatting problem. We had it checked against the B/C/S. It has been corrected. The B/C/S lists the correct speakers, the name of the correct speakers in accordance with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the empty box that's out now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's precisely right. And we have also adjusted and corrected the misleading pages numbers. They are now listed sequentially as appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you have copies of that transcript now for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Javier has them and can distribute them to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have a question about the date of the first transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The question there seem to be whether or not that was an omission or reflected the fact that no date could be attributed to that particular intercept. Based on my preliminary inquiries, and I say "preliminary" because I haven't satisfied myself that every possible measure has been taken to determine whether a date can be found for that particular intercept, it appears that the reason there is no date is that one cannot be determined based on the available information. There are a handful of intercepts for which that is the case, and this appears to be one. I've also made inquiries about the possibility of providing some textual date; however, at this point, the most we can say is it's an intercept from 1991 or 1992, but we're not in a position to pin it down with any greater specificity than that. And we tell the Court it was not an omission. It's a reflection of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. So we now receive the new copies of the transcript of the 11th of December 1991. Madam Registrar, could we please go through the list of the exhibits that have been tendered since the end of the recess. I don't know whether the parties have already prepared the rather long list from before the recess. We could start with that -- no. Then I'll leave it to that and just see that we get no further backlog at this moment. Madam Registrar, could you please guide us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since it's freshest in our mind, we start with the last witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit Number P265, witness statement of Ibro Osmanovic dated 5, 7, and 10 October 1994. P265.1, B/C/S translation. P266, witness statement of Ibro Osmanovic dated 7th of June 2001. P266.1, B/C/S translation. P267, Vlasenica Crisis Staff document for freedom of movement. P267.1, English translation. P268, photograph of Vlasenica town marked by witness. P269, photograph of Susica camp marked by witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't hear any objections, Ms. Loukas, so they are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, there's no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Registrar, we perhaps go back. The previous witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I can indicate -- I constantly have issues with this microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Be sure that your voice will be heard, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed. Now, Your Honour, just in relation to the document that I put forward to the Court when I was cross-examining Mr. Osmanovic, that third statement, I'll be indicating that the Defence proposes, of course, to tender that as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you'd like to have that tendered. Then that's the... That is the -- Ms. Loukas, that's the witness statement given by Ibro Osmanovic on the 11th of October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of which we received an English copy only at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. We have got three English copies, and I've also forwarded a B/C/S copy as well. But equality of arms does not extend to having a photocopier that works properly in the Defence room. So we will undertake to provide further copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, then we would already assign a number to it. Ms. Loukas, I see that the English copy is signed by the witness. Would that be the original, which is often the case where translation is made usually only later? That would be, then, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit Number D26 and D26.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And then we still hope to receive D26.1 soon. If there's no objection, then that would be admitted into evidence as well unless there would be any issue of translation, of course, that would be raised by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, let's then go back in time, the previous witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit Number P260, coloured map showing Kljuc and its borders. Exhibit P261, photograph view from Karanfil Osmanovic's house of house of Sefik Medanovic. P262, photograph view of ruin of Karanfil Osmanovic's house. P263, photograph view of Sefik Medanovic's house showing ruin of Karanfil Osmanovic's house. P264, list made by the Kljuc Army of those captured, killed in Prhovo. P264.1, English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since I hear no objections, these exhibits are admitted into evidence. Madam Registrar, going back -- further back in time.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Witness Redzic exhibits: Exhibit P258, protocol of the agreement on the territorial partition of Vlasenica Municipality and the establishment of new municipalities between representatives of Serbian and Muslim Peoples as authorised by representatives of parliamentary parties and the Council for Interethnic Cooperation dated 11 April 1992. P258.1, English translation. P259, authentication sheet by Witness Redzic of five recorded telephone intercepts. P259A, CD of intercepted conversations. P259B, transcripts of P259A. And P259.1, English translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Is there any objection? If there's not, these documents are admitted into evidence. Mr. Tieger, it goes without saying that without a date, that one transcript, of course, might have less probative value than with a date. So the Chamber invites you to come up with any further information about or any further evidence relating to the date of that transcript. Then we have gone through the exhibits. We have approximately 15 minutes left. It was indicated that there were still some summaries to be read into the transcript. It was even asked to do that on Thursday, but Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond it's now Wednesday, and we are already at a point that we have some time left.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, I apologise. It seems to me that I should have anticipated at least the possibility of concluding early and being able to use this time for that purpose. The only thing I can suggest at this point is that we see how quickly Ms. Javier can retrieve them. However, under the circumstances, I'm not entirely sure that's what we would want to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would like to turn -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we do that, I would just indicate that it was indicated to me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please also direct the microphone in your...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I think this microphone is the bane of my existence, Your Honour. Back in Australia, fortunately, we don't have to turn these things on and off. Just in relation to that, it was just indicated to me and, of course it's unfortunate and Mr. Tieger has apologised, but it was indicated to me yesterday by a member of the Prosecution team that they thought that it was possible that we might finish early and that they would have the summaries ready. But I'm sure the Court, as I do, accept Mr. Tieger's apology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you do, Ms. Loukas, how could the Court refrain from accepting the apologies of Mr. Tieger. I'd like to turn into -- one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has nothing further at this very moment the Chamber would like to raise. Therefore, we'll -- may I ask you, Mr. Tieger, do you have a witness for tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we could start. I think we're sitting in the morning tomorrow. We could start at 9.00. And so we'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, same courtroom, Madam Registrar, 9.00.
